title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Replication
summary: The durability/latency trade-off behind every replication choice, and what replication lag does to reads.

slides.markdown:
Once you've picked [a replication strategy](replication-strategies) — say, single-leader — there's a second, independent decision: does the leader wait for followers to confirm a write before telling the client it succeeded?

Wait for confirmation and you get durability at the cost of latency (**synchronous**). Don't wait, and you get fast writes but risk followers falling behind (**asynchronous**). This topic covers that trade-off and the very real consequence — replication lag — that asynchronous replication accepts.

slides.sectionTitle: Synchronous replication: durability at the cost of latency
slides.markdown:
In **synchronous replication**, the leader waits for one or more followers to confirm they've written the data before it reports success back to the client. If the leader dies immediately after, at least one follower is guaranteed to have the latest write — nothing is lost.

The cost is that every write now takes as long as the slowest follower you're waiting on, plus the network round trip to it. If a follower is in another region, that can add tens to hundreds of milliseconds to every single write.

This is the right default when losing a just-acknowledged write is unacceptable — financial ledgers, order placement — and you can afford the latency.

slides.sectionTitle: Asynchronous replication: fast writes, replication lag risk
slides.markdown:
In **asynchronous replication**, the leader reports success as soon as *it* has durably written the data, without waiting for any follower. Writes are fast — latency is whatever the leader alone takes, with no dependency on follower speed or distance.

The risk this accepts: if the leader fails before a write reaches any follower, that write is gone permanently, even though the client was already told it succeeded. Followers can also simply lag behind under load, serving reads that are seconds (or more) out of date.

Most systems default to asynchronous for its speed, and only pay for synchronous where a lost acknowledged write would be a real incident.

The timelines make the trade-off literal: synchronous replication's client-visible latency includes a full round trip to a follower, while asynchronous replication's client-visible latency stops at the leader — the follower catches up afterward, on its own schedule.

slides.sectionTitle: Replication lag: what it does to read-after-write behavior
slides.markdown:
**Replication lag** is the delay between a write landing on the leader and that write showing up on a follower. It's the direct, visible consequence of choosing asynchronous replication — and it's what causes the "I just posted this and now it's gone" bug: the client writes to the leader, then a subsequent read gets routed to a lagging follower.

Lag isn't constant — it grows under write-heavy load, network congestion, or a follower that's momentarily busy (say, running a backup), and can spike from milliseconds to minutes without warning.

Systems that care about this route a user's own post-write reads back to the leader (or a replica known to be caught up) for a short window, rather than accepting whatever follower the load balancer happens to pick.

slides.sectionTitle: Semi-synchronous replication as the middle ground
slides.markdown:
**Semi-synchronous replication** waits for confirmation from just *one* follower (not all of them) before acknowledging the write, while the rest replicate asynchronously in the background. This guarantees the write survives the leader failing, without paying the latency cost of waiting on every replica — only the slowest of the *many* becomes the slowest of *one*.

MySQL's semi-sync replication and many managed Postgres offerings (a synchronous standby plus async read replicas) use exactly this pattern in production.

It's a pragmatic default: most of synchronous's durability guarantee, most of asynchronous's speed.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: sync vs async vs semi-sync on durability, latency, complexity
slides.markdown:
| | Synchronous | Asynchronous | Semi-synchronous |
|---|---|---|---|
| Durability if leader dies right after ack | Guaranteed — a follower has it | At risk — the write can be lost entirely | Guaranteed — one follower confirmed |
| Write latency | Highest — waits on the slowest follower | Lowest — leader alone | Moderate — waits on the fastest one follower |
| Failure mode under a slow follower | Every write slows down | Unaffected — follower just lags further | Unaffected, as long as one follower keeps up |
| Typical use | Financial ledgers, order placement | Social feeds, analytics events | General-purpose default for many managed databases |

**How to decide:** ask what a lost just-acknowledged write actually costs. If the honest answer is "a support ticket," go async or semi-sync; if it's "a compliance incident," pay for synchronous.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reading from a lagging replica right after writing to the leader
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We use read replicas for scale, and it doesn't matter which one a request hits since they're all copies of the same data."

**Why it's wrong:** under asynchronous replication, "copies of the same data" is only true after replication lag closes — a replica can be milliseconds to minutes behind the leader. A client that writes, then immediately reads from a load-balanced replica, can see the *pre-write* state and reasonably conclude their write failed.

**Correct model:** for reads that must reflect a user's own recent write, either route them to the leader, pin them to the replica that served the write, or track replication position and wait for a replica to catch up before reading from it. Don't treat "read replica" as synonymous with "identical, up-to-date copy."

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: measuring and budgeting for lag in production
slides.markdown:
Replication lag isn't abstract — production systems expose it as a metric, and on-call engineers watch it directly. Postgres exposes it via `pg_stat_replication` (bytes of write-ahead log the replica hasn't applied yet); MySQL's `SHOW REPLICA STATUS` reports `Seconds_Behind_Source` directly.

Healthy lag on a well-provisioned system is usually **under 1 second**. A replica falling behind by 10+ seconds is a signal something's wrong — an underpowered replica, a burst of large writes, or a long-running query blocking replay — and by 60+ seconds, most teams treat it as an incident: stale reads are now visible to real users, and a leader failover at that moment would lose up to a minute of writes.

The number to actually set as an alert threshold is workload-specific, but the discipline is universal: pick a lag budget *before* you need it (e.g. "page if any replica exceeds 5s for more than 2 minutes"), because by the time lag is visible in a support ticket, it's already been a problem for a while.
